title: The Promise of Return and the Fall of Babylon
english: …remained hard and disobedient, and lived a loathsome and utterly lawless life. So the God of all, in His wise ordering, after the blow and the scourges and the things that had befallen them at the hands of their enemies from time to time, foretells also things most pleasant and able to gladden them. He promises that He will bring back home even those already taken captive, will release them from the bonds of their misery, and will hand over to their enemies those very people who had once conquered them.

For it was surely very likely that, even if they had stayed uncorrected by the earlier things, they would at least now be delighted by the later ones, take wing toward the hope of what they longed for, and choose from then on to honour the worship dearest to God and keep their mind unshaken toward Him.

Many had sacked the land of the Jews at various times, but the harshest and fiercest of all were above all the Chaldeans and those who reigned over Babylon in their turn. So the word of prophecy leaps on them first, as it were, and says: “Raise a signal on a mountain of the plain” (Isaiah 13:2).

Since we have chosen to give an exact account in interpreting the passage before us, I think we must first relate some of the most necessary facts. Cyrus, then, son of Cambyses by his father and of Mandane by his mother, who reigned over the Persians and the Medes, marched against Babylon and against the whole land of the Chaldeans, which was wide and very large, and he conquered it.

He did not take it by his own forces, nor because he could use a stronger hand, for the Chaldean nation was unbeatable and without rival because of its numbers and its thorough training in warfare. Rather, God put his opponents under him and shook down the ungodly power of the Babylonians. He did this because sorcery abounded among them beyond measure and the swarm of their idols was past counting. Indeed, it has been called “the land of carved images” (Jeremiah 50:38), either because of the multitude of idols or because each of those who lived there was found to differ in no way from an idol, I mean in turning aside to error without check or restraint.

Besides this, He did it because they laid waste the holy land allotted to God, that is, Judaea, burned Jerusalem and the divine temple itself, carried off the sacred vessels to their own land, and in unrestrained fury killed Israel, though it was called a holy people, the portion and lot of God. That God handed Israel over into the hands of enemies when it worshipped idols is not unclear to those who know the sacred writings; but they punished him beyond measure…

title: Beasts and Echoes in Ruined Babylon
english: …of those in it, because it has been laid utterly waste. It should be known that he calls “Arabs” the Saracen tribes, which reach as far as the land of the Assyrians itself and occupy the innermost desert; for they have the land of the Arabs as their neighbour. And it is likely that the Saracens from Arabia themselves also roam, mingled together, through the deserts of the Assyrians.

“And wild beasts will rest there, and the houses will be filled with echo. And sirens will rest there, and demons will dance there. And donkey-centaurs will dwell there, and hedgehogs will make their nests in their houses. It comes quickly and will not delay” (Isaiah 13:21-22).

Wild animals somehow always like to make deserted places their home, and a city falling into ruin gives them a great many hiding places, wide ones too, roofed over by themselves and makeshift, found, as it were, by chance and of their own accord. In deserts and silent places a faint echo, I do not know how, rises as if out of the very depth of the silence and steals into the ears of those who keep still.

So wild beasts, he says, will rest there, and the houses will be filled with echo; that is, having no one at all living in them, they will come to hold the echo that belongs to desolate places. And demons too, he says, will dance there. For they say that these also especially like to linger in quiet places and to make them a kind of leisurely lodging.

By “sirens” he means, I think, the birds that know how to sing sweetly, or, according to the Hebrew edition, the owl. The wild donkeys he has called “donkey-centaurs”; and by “hedgehogs” he means those mice that bristle, as it were, with sharp spines. All these would fittingly suit cities or houses that are wholly deserted.

To these he adds that “it comes quickly and will not delay” (Isaiah 13:22). He does this either to put a sharper anxiety into the Assyrians, or else to make it no small comfort to those of Israel's blood. For since they were in captivity and were expecting to be set free when Cyrus marched against the land of the Babylonians with the Persians and the Medes, he promises them a swift release from their troubles: what they prayed for would not be put off for long, but would follow, as it were, close on the heels of the word.

“And the Lord will have mercy on Jacob and will yet choose Israel, and they will rest on their own land, and the sojourner will be joined to them and will be joined to the house of Jacob. And nations will take them and bring them into their place; and they will take possession of them, and they will be multiplied on the land of God as male and female slaves. And those who took them captive will be captives, and those who ruled over them will be ruled. And it will be on that day…” (Isaiah 14:1-3).

title: Why Babylon Was Punished
english: …the Lord's portion is His people Jacob, Israel the measured lot of His inheritance” (Deuteronomy 32:9). It is therefore a most terrible thing to rise up against the land of the Lord, that is, the Church, and to carry out murderous outrages against the people allotted to Christ. For whoever is caught in such monstrous crimes will in no way be held guiltless.

But someone, I think, who has considered the calamities that befell Judaea and Jerusalem itself might say: “Did the tyrant of the Babylonians come of his own accord, march against the land of the Jews and take the holy city, without God letting him do it, or rather without God giving it to him? Yet the prophet Isaiah himself tells us: ‘The Lord will whistle for the fly that rules part of the river of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of the Assyrians, and they will all come and rest in the ravines of the land, and in the holes of the rocks, and in the caves, and in every cleft, and on every tree’ (Isaiah 7:18-19). How then can the Babylonian, who served God's command, bear a charge he cannot escape, and be punished so terribly that nothing can be seen beyond the wrath brought upon him?”

Yes, and with very good reason. For the God of all willed to rebuke Israel when he had turned aside to apostasy, and by measured chastisements to persuade him to run back to the worship he was used to, I mean the worship of the Law. But the Babylonian, though brought in for this purpose, was merciless like a wild beast and gave free rein to his fury. So he is accused, as God says plainly: “I have been jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion with great jealousy, and with great anger I am angry with the nations that join in the attack; for I was angry only a little, but they joined in the attack for evil” (Zechariah 1:14-15).

God raised up Pharaoh, who was a vessel of anger and wrath (Romans 9:22) and was already liable to punishment for his own offences, so that, as He Himself says, He might show in him His own power and the exactness of His just judgment (Romans 9:17; Exodus 9:16). In the same way you should understand the case of the Babylonians. They were vessels of wrath who justly deserved punishment, and they were brought against Jerusalem so that, after disciplining Israel, they too might afterward be given up to the punishment that most befitted and best suited them.

“Wicked seed, prepare your children to be slaughtered for the sins of your father, so that they may not rise up and fill the earth with wars. And I will rise up against them, says the Lord of Hosts, and I will destroy their name and remnant and seed” (Isaiah 14:20-22).
